body.en: The final 10 to 15 questions of the ACT Math test regularly introduce advanced precalculus and algebra topics: complex numbers, matrices, vector mechanics, logarithms, and sequence series. Mastering these ensures reaching the competitive 30–36 score band.

label.en: Definition 8.1 — Complex Numbers, Modulus, and Conjugate Division

body.en:
The imaginary unit \(i\) satisfies \(i^2 = -1\) (or \(i = \sqrt{-1}\)):
  • Cyclic Powers of \(i\) (Period 4):
    \[ i^1 = i, \quad i^2 = -1, \quad i^3 = -i, \quad i^4 = 1 \]\[ i^n = i^{n \pmod 4} \]
  • Complex Arithmetic & Modulus: For \(z = a + bi\):
    Modulus (distance from origin in Argand plane): \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\).
    Complex Conjugate: \(\bar{z} = a - bi\), satisfying \(z \cdot \bar{z} = a^2 + b^2\).
  • Division via Rationalization:
    \[ \frac{a + bi}{c + di} = \frac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{(c + di)(c - di)} = \frac{(ac + bd) + (bc - ad)i}{c^2 + d^2} \]

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers

body.en: Algebraic & Geometric Duality of \(\mathbb{C}\): Every complex number \(z = x + iy\) corresponds bijectively to a point \((x, y)\) in the Argand plane with modulus \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and principal argument \(\theta = \arg(z) \in (-\pi, \pi]\). In exponential Euler form, \(z = re^{i\theta} = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), multiplication scales moduli and adds arguments: \(z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}\).

label.en: Theorem 8.1 — Matrix Operations, Vectors, and Logarithms

body.en:
Advanced ACT test specifications:
  • Matrix Multiplication & Determinant:
    Dimension compatibility: \((m \times k) \times (k \times n) = (m \times n)\). Inner dimensions must match.
    Determinant of \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\):
    \[ \det(A) = ad - bc \]
    Inverse exists if and only if \(\det(A) \neq 0\):
    \[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix} \]
  • 2D Vectors: For \(\vec{u} = \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle\) and \(\vec{v} = \langle v_1, v_2 \rangle\):
    Magnitude: \(\|\vec{v}\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2}\).
    Dot Product: \(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2\). If \(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = 0\), vectors are perpendicular.
  • Logarithmic Laws: \(\log_b(x) = y \iff b^y = x\):
    \[ \log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y, \quad \log_b\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \log_b x - \log_b y, \quad \log_b(x^k) = k\log_b x \]
  • Sequences and Series:
    Arithmetic: \(a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d\), \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\).
    Geometric: \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\), \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\) for \(|r| < 1\).

• Matrix Dimensions for Multiplication: To multiply \( A_{m imes k} imes B_{k imes n} \), the inner dimensions MUST match (number of columns of \(A\) = number of rows of \(B\)). The product has dimensions \( m imes n \). Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: \( AB eq BA \) in general.
  • Matrix Determinant & Inverse: For a \( 2 imes 2 \) matrix \( egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} \), \( \det(A) = ad - bc \). If \( \det(A) = 0 \), the matrix has NO inverse. To form \( A^{-1} = rac{1}{ad-bc} egin{pmatrix} d & -b \ -c & a \end{pmatrix} \), swap the main diagonal and negate the off-diagonal entries!
  • Powers of \( i \) Cycle of 4: \( i^1 = i \), \( i^2 = -1 \), \( i^3 = -i \), \( i^4 = 1 \). To evaluate \( i^n \), divide \( n \) by 4 and look at the remainder: remainder 0 \( \implies 1 \), remainder 1 \( \implies i \), remainder 2 \( \implies -1 \), remainder 3 \( \implies -i \).
  • Logarithm False Rules: Remember \(\log(a + b) eq \log a + \log b\), and \( rac{\log a}{\log b} eq \log(a - b)\). Only products inside a single logarithm expand into sums.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers)

body.en:
Why De Moivre's Theorem & Conjugate Root Pairing Hold: By Euler's identity \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), raising \(z = re^{i\theta}\) to the \(n\)-th power gives:

\[ z^n = \left(re^{i\theta}\right)^n = r^n e^{in\theta} = r^n(\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)) \]

Furthermore, if \(P(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k\) has real coefficients (\(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\)), taking complex conjugates across \(P(z_0) = 0\) uses \(\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar{z}_1 + \bar{z}_2\) and \(\bar{a}_k = a_k\) to prove \(P(\bar{z}_0) = \overline{P(z_0)} = 0\). Thus non-real roots of real polynomials always occur in conjugate pairs \(\alpha \pm i\beta\).

label.en: Worked Example 8.A — Complex Fraction Division and Rationalization

body.en:
Simplify the expression \(\dfrac{5 + 2i}{3 - 4i}\) and write the result in standard complex form \(a + bi\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Identify the complex conjugate of the denominator \(3 - 4i\): The conjugate is \(3 + 4i\).
  2. Multiply numerator and denominator by \(3 + 4i\):
    \[ \frac{5 + 2i}{3 - 4i} \cdot \frac{3 + 4i}{3 + 4i} = \frac{(5 + 2i)(3 + 4i)}{(3 - 4i)(3 + 4i)} \]
  3. Expand the denominator using \((c - di)(c + di) = c^2 + d^2\):
    \[ 3^2 - (4i)^2 = 9 - 16(-1) = 9 + 16 = 25 \]
  4. Expand the numerator using FOIL:
    \[ 5(3) + 5(4i) + 2i(3) + 2i(4i) = 15 + 20i + 6i + 8i^2 \]\[ = 15 + 26i + 8(-1) = 7 + 26i \]
  5. Divide each term by the real denominator \(25\):
    \[ \frac{7 + 26i}{25} = \frac{7}{25} + \frac{26}{25}i \]
The simplified expression in standard \(a + bi\) form is \(\mathbf{\frac{7}{25} + \frac{26}{25}i}\).

label.en: Worked Example 8.B — Logarithmic Equation with Change of Base

body.en:
Solve for \(x\): \(\log_2(x) + \log_2(x - 6) = 4\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Combine logarithms using the product property \(\log_b A + \log_b B = \log_b(AB)\):
    \[ \log_2(x(x - 6)) = 4 \]
  2. Rewrite in exponential form \(b^y = \text{argument}\):
    \[ x(x - 6) = 2^4 = 16 \]
  3. Expand into a standard quadratic equation:
    \[ x^2 - 6x - 16 = 0 \]
  4. Factor the quadratic:
    \[ (x - 8)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = 8 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -2 \]
  5. Check for extraneous solutions against domain restrictions \(x > 0\) and \(x - 6 > 0 \implies x > 6\):
    For \(x = -2\): \(\log_2(-2)\) is undefined.
    For \(x = 8\): \(\log_2(8) + \log_2(2) = 3 + 1 = 4\) (valid).
The unique valid solution is \(\mathbf{x = 8}\).

label.en: Worked Example 8.C — 2x2 Matrix Determinant & Singular Matrix Condition

body.en:
For what value of \(k\) does the matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & k \\ 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}\) fail to have an inverse?

Solution: A \(2 \times 2\) matrix is singular (non-invertible) when \(\det(A) = ad - bc = 0\):
\[ 6(8) - 4k = 0 \implies 48 = 4k \implies \mathbf{k = 12} \]

label.en: Worked Example 8.D — Infinite Geometric Series Convergence

body.en:
Find the sum of the infinite geometric series \(18 + 6 + 2 + \frac{2}{3} + \cdots\).

Solution: Here \(a_1 = 18\) and common ratio \(r = \frac{6}{18} = \frac{1}{3}\). Since \(|r| < 1\):
\[ S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r} = \frac{18}{1 - 1/3} = \frac{18}{2/3} = \mathbf{27} \]

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers)

rows.en: Places a 2nd-quadrant complex number in the 4th quadrant.
Forgets \(i^2 = -1\), flipping the sign of \(bd\) in the real part.
Group real and imaginary parts carefully: \((ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i\).
Fails to rewrite in standard form \(|z - z_0| = r\).
Factor out the minus sign: \(|z - (-4 + 6i)| = 4 \implies z_0 = (-4, 6)\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers

body.en: Exam Verification Tip (ACT Mathematics Test): Always check complex division \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\) by verifying that \(|z_1 / z_2| = |z_1| / |z_2|\). If the moduli ratio does not match, you multiplied the denominator by \(a + bi\) instead of the conjugate \(a - bi\).

question.en: Simplify \((2+3i)(1-i)\) and write in the standard form \(a+bi\).

solution.en:
Multiply using FOIL:
\[ (2+3i)(1-i) = 2(1) - 2i + 3i - 3i^2 = 2 + i - 3(-1) = 2 + i + 3 = \mathbf{5 + i} \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Isolate the primary variable or parameter systematically and simplify like terms before substituting numerical values.
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: If \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}\), what is the matrix product \(AB\)?

solution.en:
The product of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix and a \(2 \times 1\) matrix is a \(2 \times 1\) column vector. Compute row by column:
First row: \(2(5) + (-1)(-2) = 10 + 2 = 12\).
Second row: \(3(5) + 4(-2) = 15 - 8 = 7\).
Thus \(AB = \mathbf{\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}}\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers and start from \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(2 \times 2\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: What is the value of the complex expression \(i^{47} - i^{18}\)?

solution.en:
Divide exponents by 4:
\(47 = 4(11) + 3 \implies i^{47} = i^3 = -i\).
\(18 = 4(4) + 2 \implies i^{18} = i^2 = -1\).
Therefore:
\[ i^{47} - i^{18} = -i - (-1) = \mathbf{1 - i} \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Matrices, Vectors & Complex Numbers and start from \(i^{47} - i^{18}\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(47 = 4(11) + 3 \implies i^{47} = i^3 = -i\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: An infinite geometric sequence has first term \(a_1 = 18\) and common ratio \(r = -\frac{1}{3}\). What is the sum of this infinite series?

solution.en:
Since \(|r| = |-\frac{1}{3}| < 1\), the infinite series converges. Using the formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\):
\[ S_\infty = \frac{18}{1 - (-1/3)} = \frac{18}{1 + 1/3} = \frac{18}{4/3} = 18 \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{54}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{27}{2}} \text{ (or } 13.5\text{)} \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(|r| = |-\frac{1}{3}| < 1\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.
